rationale: A wins because it gives the founder three usable lanes and keeps the missing proof visible instead of painting scenery on it. A's "The DTC darling that quietly became a wholesale company" is anchored to the real channel shift and then admits, "without a number this stays a claim, not a proven contrarian story." B has good instincts, but "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" and "the one who never made it to the prestige mall" turn assumptions into copy. That is how a smart pitch becomes a reporter's first correction.
gaps_in_A: "collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" is bigger than the supplied facts prove; it needs category evidence beyond Glossier's own channel claim.
"Glossier was a poster child for DTC-only branding" relies on outside reputation, not the given update. Plausible, but still not supplied.
"A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" makes the fragrance launch sound strategic before the facts show why scent and shelf expansion belong together.
The retail scale angle knows its own hole: "context on how 1,400 doors compares to other prestige brands in Sephora" is necessary before the door count means much.
gaps_in_B: "after a decade of treating retail as the enemy" is invented. DTC-only is not the same as anti-retail, and a reporter will ask you to prove it.
The first two angles are padded twins: "wholesale is now its fastest-growing channel" and "calling wholesale its fastest-growing channel" are the same DTC-reversal story in two jackets.
"the one who never made it to the prestige mall" decorates the Sephora-at-Kohl's fact with an unsupported shopper narrative.
"targets a geographic and demographic profile that standalone Sephora does not reach" is a claim, not a fact from the update. B lists the proof it would need, but says the thing anyway.
